newsitem.title: USA: Study sees benefit to removing cancerous prostate.
newsitem.headline: Study sees benefit to removing cancerous prostate.

text.p: Removing a cancerous prostate gland produces good overall survival rates, although questions remain about how to treat the most common cancer diagnosed among American men, researchers said on Tuesday.

Between 60 percent and 97 percent of men who undergo radical prostatectomy survive for 10 years after the surgery, depending on the stage and grade of the cancer, researchers at the University of Miami School of Medicine and the Veterans Affairs Medical Centre in Miami wrote in the Journal of the American Medical Association.

Prostate cancer afflicts nearly 10 out of 100,000 American males, many in old age when surgery or radiation treatment can be avoided. Some men diagnosed with this cancer, especially older men, undergo radiation therapy while others adopt a "watchful waiting" position to monitor spread of the disease.
"One should be extremely cautious about using the present observations in making inferences about relative treatment effectiveness," study author Arnon Krongrad wrote.

The researchers analysed data on 3,626 patients in nine regions of the United States and found no geographical variations in mortality rates from the disease. But older men and black men were associated with worse overall 10-year survival rates, though not necessarily caused by the cancer.

The study showed that prostate surgery among men whose cancer had not spread and who had more normal-appearing cells present had "excellent disease-specific survival, which is associated with relatively good overall survival."
The prostate provides lubrication to the urethra and supplies semen for ejaculation.
